plan.planning_summary: This portfolio tests three distinct strategy axes for achieving spectral selectivity in thermal infrared emission using only HfO2/SiO2 dielectric stacks on silicon. Route 1 explores periodic quarter-wave Bragg stacks tuned to the 8-13 μm atmospheric window, leveraging constructive interference for high emissivity in the target band. Route 2 tests aperiodic thickness distributions that may broaden the high-emissivity band while maintaining suppression in 3-5 μm. Route 3 investigates a defect-cavity microresonator structure that creates a narrow high-emissivity peak within the atmospheric window. These axes are chosen because they represent fundamentally different physical mechanisms (Bragg reflection vs. graded impedance vs. cavity resonance) that could succeed or fail independently. Literature L01, L04, L11, L16, and L20 support the general approach of multilayer spectral selectivity for thermal management, but none prescribe the exact topology, so each route states its hypothesis clearly.

routes.title: Periodic Quarter-Wave Bragg Stack for 8-13 μm High Emissivity
routes.scientific_hypothesis: A periodic alternating HfO2/SiO2 quarter-wave stack tuned to the center of the 8-13 μm atmospheric window will produce high emissivity in that band through constructive interference while suppressing emissivity in the 3-5 μm band through destructive interference.
routes.design_principle: Quarter-wave optical thickness layers create a photonic bandgap where reflectance is minimized (emissivity maximized) at the design wavelength and its harmonics. By centering the stack at ~10.5 μm, the fundamental resonance falls within the atmospheric window while the 3-5 μm band lies outside the high-emissivity region.
routes.proposed_topology: air | (hfo2 | sio2)_6 | si substrate, exactly 12 layers total (6 pairs)
design_variables: individual layer thicknesses for all 12 layers, starting from quarter-wave at 10500 nm center wavelength
soft_objectives: maximize mean emissivity in 8000-13000 nm band
minimize mean emissivity in 3000-5000 nm band
maintain total layer count at exactly 12
manufacturing_considerations: 12 layers is well within the 24-layer limit
quarter-wave thicknesses at 10.5 μm are physically realizable (hundreds of nm to microns)
HfO2 and SiO2 are standard deposition materials
theory_basis: Transfer matrix method for multilayer interference
Kirchhoff's law relating emissivity to absorptance
expected_advantages: Simple periodic structure is easy to fabricate
Literature L16 and L20 support multilayer selective emitter approach
known_risks: Periodic stacks produce narrowband response that may not cover full 8-13 μm window
Higher-order harmonics could create unwanted emissivity peaks in 3-5 μm band
Fixed pair count may limit achievable selectivity
routes.execution_request_english: Design a periodic multilayer dielectric stack on silicon substrate with air incidence. Stack structure: air | (hfo2 | SiO2 (Kischkat))_6 | si, exactly 12 layers total. Optimize individual layer thicknesses for all 12 layers, initialized at quarter-wave optical thickness for 10500 nm center wavelength. Target: maximize emissivity in 8000-13000 nm band, minimize emissivity in 3000-5000 nm band. Wavelength range for evaluation: 3000-13000 nm. Polarization: unpolarized (average TE and TM). Incidence angle: 0 degrees (normal). Material refractive indices from catalog datasets for hfo2, SiO2 (Kischkat), and si. Total layer count fixed at 12.

routes.title: Aperiodic Thickness-Graded Stack for Broadened 8-13 μm Response
routes.scientific_hypothesis: An aperiodic HfO2/SiO2 stack with chirped (graded) layer thicknesses will produce broader high-emissivity coverage across the full 8-13 μm atmospheric window compared to a periodic stack, while maintaining low emissivity in 3-5 μm.
routes.design_principle: Varying layer thicknesses across the stack creates multiple overlapping resonances that broaden the high-emissivity band. Gradually changing optical thickness from front to back of the stack can create an impedance-matched transition that reduces reflection across a wider wavelength range.
routes.proposed_topology: air | hfo2 | sio2 | hfo2 | sio2 | hfo2 | sio2 | hfo2 | sio2 | hfo2 | sio2 | hfo2 | sio2 | hfo2 | sio2 | hfo2 | sio2 | hfo2 | sio2 | hfo2 | sio2 | hfo2 | sio2 | hfo2 | sio2 | si substrate, exactly 24 layers total (12 pairs)
design_variables: individual layer thicknesses for all 24 layers, initialized with linear chirp from 8000 nm to 13000 nm quarter-wave values
soft_objectives: maximize mean emissivity in 8000-13000 nm band
minimize mean emissivity in 3000-5000 nm band
maximize spectral uniformity (minimize variance) within 8000-13000 nm band
manufacturing_considerations: 24 layers uses the maximum allowed layer count
chirped thicknesses require precise deposition control
HfO2 and SiO2 are compatible with standard thin-film processes
theory_basis: Impedance matching through graded index structures
Multiple resonance superposition for bandwidth broadening
Literature L04 and L11 on dual-selective emitters
expected_advantages: Full 24-layer budget allows more degrees of freedom for optimization
Chirped design may achieve broader band coverage than periodic approach
Literature L04 supports dual-selective emitter concept
known_risks: More layers increase fabrication complexity and potential for defects
Aperiodic optimization may converge to local minima
L22 notes temperature-dependent effects not modeled here

Stack structure: air | (hfo2 | SiO2 (Kischkat))_12 | si, exactly 24 layers total. Optimize individual layer thicknesses for all 24 layers, initialized with linear chirp from quarter-wave at 8000 nm (front) to quarter-wave at 13000 nm (back). Target: maximize mean emissivity in 8000-13000 nm band, minimize mean emissivity in 3000-5000 nm band, maximize spectral uniformity within 8000-13000 nm. Wavelength range for evaluation: 3000-13000 nm. Polarization: unpolarized (average TE and TM). Incidence angle: 0 degrees (normal). Material refractive indices from catalog datasets for hfo2, SiO2 (Kischkat), and si. Total layer count fixed at 24.

routes.title: Defect Cavity Microresonator for Narrowband 8-13 μm Peak
routes.scientific_hypothesis: A Fabry-Perot microcavity formed by HfO2/SiO2 Bragg mirrors with a central defect layer will produce a sharp high-emissivity resonance within the 8-13 μm atmospheric window while maintaining very low emissivity outside the resonance, including the 3-5 μm band.
routes.design_principle: Two Bragg mirror stacks sandwich a cavity layer whose optical thickness creates a resonant mode within the mirror bandgap. This produces a narrow transmission (high emissivity) peak at the cavity resonance wavelength while the mirrors suppress emission elsewhere.
routes.proposed_topology: air | (hfo2 | sio2)_4 | hfo2 (cavity) | (sio2 | hfo2)_4 | si substrate, exactly 17 layers total (8 mirror layers + 1 cavity + 8 mirror layers)
design_variables: mirror layer thicknesses (8 pairs, 16 layers) at quarter-wave for 10500 nm, cavity layer thickness (1 layer) tuned for resonance position within 8000-13000 nm
soft_objectives: maximize peak emissivity at cavity resonance within 8000-13000 nm
position resonance near 10500 nm center of atmospheric window
manufacturing_considerations: cavity thickness precision critical for resonance positioning
Bragg mirrors require consistent layer thickness control
theory_basis: Defect mode in photonic bandgap structures
Literature L08 on quasi-optical microcavity, L19 on resonator structures for emissivity tuning
expected_advantages: Very high peak emissivity achievable at resonance
Literature L08 and L19 support microcavity approach for spectral control
known_risks: Narrow resonance may not cover full 8-13 μm window, reducing integrated emissivity
Resonance position sensitive to thickness errors
L19 notes phase-change materials not used here, limiting tunability
routes.execution_request_english: Design a defect-cavity multilayer dielectric stack on silicon substrate with air incidence. Stack structure: air | (hfo2 | SiO2 (Kischkat))_4 | hfo2_cavity | (SiO2 (Kischkat) | hfo2)_4 | si, exactly 17 layers total. Optimize mirror layer thicknesses (16 layers) at quarter-wave for 10500 nm, and cavity layer thickness (1 layer) to position resonance within 8000-13000 nm band. Target: maximize peak emissivity at resonance, minimize emissivity in 3000-5000 nm band. Wavelength range for evaluation: 3000-13000 nm. Polarization: unpolarized (average TE and TM). Incidence angle: 0 degrees (normal). Material refractive indices from catalog datasets for hfo2, SiO2 (Kischkat), and si. Total layer count fixed at 17.

routes.title: DBR-based spectral emissivity selector tuned to 3-5 μm reflection band
routes.scientific_hypothesis: A quarter-wave stack centered at 4 μm using HfO2/SiO2 pairs will produce high reflectance (low emissivity) in the 3-5 μm band while maintaining sufficient transmittance to allow silicon substrate emission in the 8-13 μm band.
routes.design_principle: Distributed Bragg reflectors create stopbands where reflectance is high when layer optical thicknesses satisfy the quarter-wave condition at a center wavelength. Emissivity equals absorptance per Kirchhoff's law, so high reflectance corresponds to low emissivity. By tuning the Bragg center to 3-5 μm, the stack should suppress emission there while remaining relatively transparent at longer wavelengths where the optical thickness no longer satisfies the Bragg condition.
routes.proposed_topology: air | hfo2 | sio2 | hfo2 | sio2 | hfo2 | sio2 | hfo2 | sio2 | hfo2 | sio2 | hfo2 | sio2 | hfo2 | sio2 | hfo2 | sio2 | hfo2 | sio2 | hfo2 | sio2 | si
soft_objectives: maximize mean emissivity in 8000-13000 nm band
minimize mean emissivity in 3000-5000 nm band
maintain smooth spectral response without sharp resonant spikes
manufacturing_considerations: total layer count is 20, within the 24 layer limit
all layers are dielectric materials compatible with standard deposition
individual layer thicknesses should remain in practical deposition range (tens to thousands of nm)
theory_basis: Recalled: Quarter-wave stacks produce maximum reflectance when each layer optical thickness equals λ/4 at the design wavelength
Recalled: HfO2 has higher refractive index than SiO2 in the infrared, providing index contrast for Bragg reflection
Recalled: Emissivity equals absorptance for opaque or semi-opaque systems per Kirchhoff's law of thermal radiation
Recalled: Bragg stopband width increases with refractive index contrast between alternating layers
Recalled: Silicon substrate is absorptive in the thermal IR and will contribute to emission if the overlying stack is transparent
expected_advantages: Simple periodic topology reduces optimization complexity
Quarter-wave starting point provides physically reasonable initial thicknesses
20 layers provides sufficient optical depth for strong reflection in the target band
Dielectric-only stack avoids metallic absorption losses
known_risks: Uncertain: Exact refractive index values of hfo2 and sio2 at 3-13 μm wavelengths - the catalog data will determine actual optical behavior
Uncertain: Whether 10 pairs provides sufficient reflectance at 3-5 μm without excessive reflection at 8-13 μm - may need to adjust pair count
Uncertain: Silicon substrate extinction coefficient at these wavelengths affects baseline emission - catalog data required
Uncertain: Whether quarter-wave condition at 4 μm is the optimal center wavelength - 3.5 μm or 4.5 μm might perform better
Risk: If hfo2 or sio2 have significant absorption in 8-13 μm, the stack itself will emit rather than transmit substrate emission
routes.execution_request_english: Optimize a 20-layer planar multilayer dielectric stack on silicon substrate with air incidence. Stack sequence: air | hfo2 | SiO2 (Kischkat) | hfo2 | SiO2 (Kischkat) | hfo2 | SiO2 (Kischkat) | hfo2 | SiO2 (Kischkat) | hfo2 | SiO2 (Kischkat) | hfo2 | SiO2 (Kischkat) | hfo2 | SiO2 (Kischkat) | hfo2 | SiO2 (Kischkat) | hfo2 | SiO2 (Kischkat) | hfo2 | SiO2 (Kischkat) | si. All 20 dielectric layer thicknesses are independent optimization variables. Target wavelength bands: 3000-5000 nm (minimize emissivity) and 8000-13000 nm (maximize emissivity). Polarization: unpolarized or average of TE and TM. Incidence angle: 0 degrees (normal incidence). Materials: hfo2, SiO2 (Kischkat), si from catalog. Evaluate emissivity as 1 minus reflectance minus transmittance, or directly as absorptance per Kirchhoff's law. Optimize thicknesses to maximize emissivity in 8000-13000 nm while minimizing emissivity in 3000-5000 nm.

research_influence: L01 and L16 motivated the general multilayer selective emitter approach used in route_01, supporting periodic Bragg stack design for infrared stealth applications
L04 and L11 influenced route_02's dual-selective design principle, emphasizing the need for both high emission in atmospheric window and low emission elsewhere
L08 and L19 informed route_03's microcavity approach, with L08 specifically discussing quasi-optical microcavity structures for spectral selectivity
L20 reinforced the feasibility of near-perfect spectral selectivity through multilayer design, supporting all three routes' objectives
L22 was noted as a risk factor for route_02, warning that temperature-dependent effects may affect static emitter performance
unresolved_decisions: Incidence angle was not specified in the request; all routes assume normal incidence (0 degrees) as a baseline hypothesis that could be tested in future work
Polarization state was not specified; all routes use unpolarized (TE+TM average) as the default for thermal emission applications
The exact refractive index datasets for hfo2 and sio2 in the 3-13 μm range will be resolved by the material catalog at execution time
plan.stop_if_all_routes_fail: If all three routes fail to achieve best_target_score above 0.5 after exhausting their stop conditions, the fundamental constraint of using only HfO2/SiO2 dielectrics without metallic or absorbing layers may be insufficient for the required spectral selectivity; consider expanding material palette or accepting reduced performance targets.

selector_prompt.system:
You are the internal material-dataset selector inside a scientific TMM
harness. This is not route planning and you must not redesign the route.
Return exactly one JSON object and no markdown:
{"selections":[{"request_id":"material_01","selected_rank":1,"provider":"rii_sqlite","dataset_id":562,"reason":"..."}]}

The user question is authoritative. Each request contains candidates already
retrieved from the local MaterialRegistry and sorted by three equal physical
metrics: target-band coverage, n/k completeness, and sampling density. Rank 1
is the most physically reliable candidate; lower rank means less reliable.
Choose exactly one candidate from the supplied list for every request. Never
invent, rename, or edit a provider or dataset_id. The selected_rank must point
to the selected array element, and provider/dataset_id must copy that element.

Material identity, stoichiometry, explicit material state/preparation, and an
explicit requested source are hard constraints. A candidate with
formula_exact=false or semantic_match=same_element_family is not an allowed
substitute for a formula request. SiO is not SiO2, even if the SiO2 candidate
has better physical coverage. When several candidates satisfy the hard
constraints, select the highest-ranked one (usually rank 1). If no candidate
satisfies them, return selected_rank:null, provider:null, dataset_id:null and
reason:"needs_confirmation" for that request.

plan.planning_summary: This control axis tests whether a distributed Bragg reflector (DBR) design tuned to reflect at 3-5 μm while remaining transparent at 8-13 μm can achieve the spectral emissivity selectivity required for thermophotovoltaic cold emitter applications. The design draws on recalled knowledge of interference-based multilayer optics: alternating high/low index dielectric layers create wavelength-selective reflectance bands. By centering the Bragg condition at approximately 4 μm, the stack should suppress emissivity in the 3-5 μm band while allowing the silicon substrate to emit in the 8-13 μm atmospheric window. This route was planned from the model's own prior knowledge alone with no literature retrieval.
